notes.meaning: The Philistine army entered Judah's territory to attack God's people, setting up camp between Socoh and Azekah. They took advantage of the weakness in Israel after Saul turned away from God. God used this dangerous invasion to create the setting where David would be raised up.

King Saul and the Israelite soldiers gathered on the other side of the valley of Elah to defend their land. The valley was named after its large terebinth trees and provided a natural stage for the battle. Both sides prepared to clash across the open ground.

The two armies stood facing each other from opposite hills, with the valley separating them. Neither side wanted to leave its high ground to attack through the ravine below. This created a tense standoff between God's chosen people and their enemies.

A huge warrior named Goliath stepped out from the Philistine camp to settle the war through single combat. He came from Gath, a city known for ancient giants, and stood over nine feet tall. He acted as a champion, fighting alone on behalf of his entire nation.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Greek copies of the Old Testament and the Dead Sea Scrolls give Goliath's height as four cubits and a span, which is just under seven feet tall.

notes.meaning: Goliath wore heavy bronze armor, including a helmet, leg guards, and a coat of scale armor weighing about one hundred and twenty-six pounds. He also carried a bronze javelin slung across his back. Though his heavy protection terrified Israel, human armor cannot protect anyone against God.

Goliath carried a spear with a wooden shaft as thick as a weaver's beam, tipped with an iron point weighing about fifteen pounds. A servant walked ahead of him carrying a full-sized shield for protection. His weapons showed that he was a soldier of extraordinary physical power.

Goliath stood before the armies and mocked the men of Israel for lining up for a full battle. He offered to decide the war through a duel, challenging Israel to choose one warrior to face him alone. This kind of single combat was meant to decide the fight without a clash between the full armies.

Goliath proposed that whichever champion won the duel, the losing nation would surrender and serve the winners. This sounded like a fair bargain, but the Philistines had no real intention of surrendering if their giant fell. He made the promise simply to trap Israel into an unfair contest.

Goliath openly defied and insulted the armies of Israel, demanding an opponent to fight him immediately. His shouts were meant to shame the Israelites and show complete contempt for their courage. By attacking Israel's army, he was also defying the God they served.

When Saul and his soldiers heard Goliath's loud challenge, they were paralyzed with terror. Saul had lost his former boldness because the Spirit of the Lord had left him, and the army followed their king's fear. When leaders take their eyes off God, entire groups of people can lose their courage.

The story introduces David, the son of an elderly man named Jesse from Bethlehem in Judah. Jesse had eight sons and was now too old to fight in Saul's army. God was preparing to use this ordinary family from a small town to deliver the whole nation.

Jesse's three oldest sons—Eliab, Abinadab, and Shammah—went off to war with King Saul. David was the youngest son and remained behind because he was not of age for military duty. While his older brothers were at the front lines, David carried out simple family chores.

David did not stay at the battlefield, but traveled back and forth between Saul's palace and his home in Bethlehem to watch his father's sheep. He had played music to comfort Saul, but returned to his quiet shepherd duties when he was not needed. This humble work trained David in faithfulness while he waited on God.

Goliath repeated his proud challenge every morning and evening for forty days straight. For more than a month, Israel sat frozen in fear while the giant disgraced them twice a day. God allowed this long delay to reveal Israel's helplessness before sending His chosen deliverer.

Jesse told David to take roasted grain, ten loaves of bread, and ten pieces of cheese to his brothers and their commanding officer. He wanted David to see how his brothers were doing and bring back a token showing they were safe. God used this normal errand of family love to place David exactly where He wanted him.

Jesse explained to David that his brothers were stationed with King Saul in the Valley of Elah, facing the Philistine army. The men stood drawn up in battle lines and ready for combat, though no fighting had started yet. Jesse simply wanted news from the front lines, unaware of what God was about to do.

David woke up early, made sure a hired keeper took care of his sheep, and carried the supplies to the army camp. He arrived just as the Israelite soldiers were marching out to their positions and shouting their war cry. Both armies lined up against each other across the valley, ready for battle.

David left his bags of food with the camp supply officer and ran quickly toward the battle line. He searched through the ranks until he found his brothers and greeted them warmly. His eagerness showed both his love for his family and his courage near danger.

While David was talking with his brothers, Goliath stepped out from the Philistine line and shouted his usual taunts. David heard the giant's arrogant words with his own ears for the first time. God arranged the timing so David would witness the disgrace directly.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that a later passage in Second Samuel states that Elhanan killed Goliath of Gath, leading them to suggest that Goliath may have been a title or that multiple traditions existed.

notes.meaning: The moment the soldiers of Israel saw Goliath walking forward, they ran away in terror. Even though they were armed for battle, the sight of the giant completely broke their spirit. Without faith in God's power, even large armies flee from physical danger.

The Israelite soldiers repeated King Saul's generous offer to anyone who could kill the giant. Saul promised great wealth, the hand of his daughter in marriage, and total tax exemption for the hero's family. Even with these huge rewards, not a single Israelite dared to step forward.

David asked the nearby soldiers what reward was promised, but his real concern was the honor of God. He asked how a pagan warrior outside God's covenant dared to insult the armies of the living God. While the soldiers saw an unbeatable giant, David saw an enemy who was nothing compared to God.

The soldiers gave David the same answer as before, confirming what the king would do for the man who defeated Goliath. David's questions made it clear that he was thinking about taking on the challenge himself. The camp buzzed with talk as the young shepherd showed interest where seasoned warriors felt only fear.

Eliab, David's oldest brother, heard him talking to the soldiers and became furious with him. He mocked David for leaving his few sheep behind and accused him of being proud, wicked, and curious just to watch the bloodshed. Eliab's anger sprang from jealousy, especially since God had passed him over to choose David as king.

David answered his brother calmly, asking what wrong he had done by simply asking an honest question. He knew there was a true cause at stake: God's honor had been insulted, and someone needed to act. David showed great self-control by refusing to trade insults with his angry brother.
